title: AI, tools and transformation — Benedict Evans
gist: Benedict Evans argues that AI will not turn everyone into a tool-builder or collapse the enterprise app stack, because the hard part was never writing code but spotting the hidden problem and then getting 50-500 people across departments and regulatory regimes to change. He reframes enterprise software as a cycle between improvised substrates (Excel, email, now chatbots) and institutionalised apps, with AI moving the thresholds rather than removing them.

insights.claim: The belief that generative AI turns every knowledge worker into a tool-builder — and therefore kills packaged apps — misreads how most people think and where software actually comes from.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Discount 'apps are dead' narratives when valuing incumbent SaaS; the death-of-apps thesis is the market's main bear case and it is weakly grounded.
insights.quote: It’s very tempting to imagine that AI turns everyone into a tool-builder - now everyone can just ask the model to make the software they need, and apps as we know them are dead.
insights.locator: It’s very tempting to imagine that AI

insights.claim: Most professionals do not instinctively think about how their own job could be done differently: a great matrimonial lawyer thinks about cases and clients, not about what great legal discovery software would do.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Self-serve AI tool-building will under-convert in verticals; distribution and problem-spotting, not model capability, is the bottleneck.
insights.locator: First of all, most people are not tool builders

insights.claim: Silicon Valley systematically overestimates AI's self-serve tool-building because everyone inside the bubble is themselves a tool-builder.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Expect a persistent gap between VC-narrative adoption curves and actual enterprise usage data.
insights.locator: If you’re a tool-builder, and everybody in Silicon Valley

insights.claim: Excel's onboarding templates were an early attempt to solve the same problem AI assistants now face, and every one of those templates went on to become a standalone company — which is why 'Claude for X' style helpers are useful but not the answer.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Vertical SaaS keeps forming even on top of general-purpose substrates; general assistants seed categories rather than absorbing them.
insights.quote: But every one of those templates still became a company, and that’s what I see in things like Claude for X as well - this is helpful, but not the answer.
insights.locator: Products like Excel try to bridge this problem

insights.claim: The bottleneck in automation is not writing code but knowing that a tool is needed at all and what it should do — so cheaper code generation does not unlock the hard part.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Coding-cost deflation alone should not be extrapolated into software TAM destruction; problem discovery remains scarce and priced.
insights.quote: The hard part is knowing that you need a tool for this in the first place, and then knowing what the tool should do.
insights.locator: None of this is solved by making easier to write code

insights.claim: Most of what software automated over recent decades was not obvious even to tool-builders: problems were hidden, bundled or embedded, and for many successful software companies there were half a dozen failed attempts before someone found the right framing.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Problem-definition risk, not build risk, still dominates early-stage software returns even in an AI-cheap-code world.
insights.locator: The deeper problem is most of what we’ve automated

insights.claim: The 'forward-deployed engineer' exists precisely because someone who knows what AI can build must physically walk around a law firm or architecture office and spot opportunities the practitioners cannot see.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: AI-application companies will carry services-heavy cost structures; model gross margins in deployment-led vendors accordingly.
insights.locator: This is what leads to the idea of the ‘forward-deployed engineer’

insights.claim: Enterprise software sits on a spectrum from top-down to bottom-up — the company buys SAP while the user makes a spreadsheet — which is better understood as a spectrum from institutionalised to improvised.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: A durable lens for sorting AI products: institutionalised tools need audit and procurement; improvised ones spread bottom-up and can be bought cheaply.
insights.locator: Second, all of this means that software is bought or chosen

insights.claim: Edge cases, exceptions and one-off questions get handled in a fuzzy improvised layer of Excel, email, shared folders, Tableau, PowerPoint, CSVs, screenshots, PDFs and conference calls.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: That improvised layer is the addressable surface most AI startups actually attack — size opportunities there, not against systems of record.
insights.locator: But then you have edge cases, exceptions and one-off questions

insights.claim: A task gets institutionalised into dedicated software once it is done repeatedly by many people and carries revenue and risk, because that is when audit, security, maintenance and accountability become mandatory.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Watch for AI workflows crossing the risk/frequency threshold — that transition is where new SaaS categories and budget lines are born.
insights.quote: You pave the desire path and pay someone to set it in stone.
insights.locator: But once this task becomes something that you're doing all the time

insights.claim: The repeated cycle of improvising a workflow and then paying to set it in stone is the reason a typical large company ends up with hundreds of applications rather than a few.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: App-count sprawl is structural, not waste — consolidation theses that assume it can be collapsed by AI tend to fail.
insights.locator: that process is why the company has hundreds of apps

insights.claim: A typical large American company runs hundreds or thousands of pieces of software — horizontal systems of record like SAP and Workday, hundreds of vertical SaaS apps, and hundreds more scripts, automations and databases down to a 10-megabyte spreadsheet running a department — and often does not know what it has or what it pays for.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Baseline for any SaaS-consolidation or spend-optimisation thesis; also explains why seat-based AI rollouts land on top of chaos.
insights.locator: The typical big American company today

insights.claim: Firm size determines the institutionalised/improvised mix: PwC hiring 3,000-4,000 graduates a year needs dedicated software, a firm hiring five or ten uses email, a shared folder and Google Sheets, and a small team inside PwC will still use Google Sheets when Workday is too inflexible.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Explains why SME SaaS and enterprise SaaS are separate markets, and why unbundling restarts inside the largest accounts.
insights.locator: Hence, if you’re PwC and you hire 3-4,000 graduates

themes.theme: Bundling, unbundling and the SaaS precedent

insights.claim: The shift to SaaS was itself an order-of-magnitude increase in how much software companies owned, plus a new operating model and cycle time, and that — not software per se — is the real reason it killed incumbents that could not make the jump.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Template for the AI transition: the casualty mechanism is operating-model and cycle-time mismatch, so screen incumbents on those, not on feature parity.
insights.locator: We went though a lot of this with the shift to SaaS

insights.claim: Everything a SaaS app does could in principle be done in SAP, Excel or email — Carta is a $4bn company that manages one spreadsheet for the CFO — and tasks sometimes migrate back the other way.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Concrete proof that value accrues to institutionalising a single workflow; a useful comp when underwriting narrow AI-native SaaS.
insights.quote: Carta is a $4bn company that manages one spreadsheet for your CFO
insights.locator: All of those SaaS apps do something

insights.claim: A consultant reported that half of their engagements were telling Excel users to move to a database and the other half were telling database users to move back to Excel.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Bundling/unbundling is oscillatory, not directional — argues against one-way 'AI collapses the stack' bets.
insights.locator: A few years ago I spoke to a consultant

insights.claim: The chatbot is best understood as a new freeform substrate sitting alongside Excel and email — taking tasks from apps and from those substrates, and also losing tasks back to them.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Frames LLM assistants as another improvisation layer, so expect a fresh institutionalisation wave of AI-native vertical apps behind it.
insights.locator: the chatbot itself is a new freeform space

insights.claim: AI does not change the buy-vs-build-vs-improvise question companies already face; it adds new choices and moves the thresholds at which a workflow graduates from a spreadsheet to a product.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: The tradeable variable is where the threshold moves — which categories get delayed graduation to SaaS and which get accelerated.
insights.quote: AI doesn’t change the question: it creates new choices and moves the thresholds.
insights.locator: AI doesn’t change the question

insights.claim: Three years into enterprise AI deployment, the pattern at big companies is that a small number of people use Copilot, ChatGPT or Claude heavily, a larger group uses it a couple of times a week, and much of the company is not really using it at all.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Seat-based AI revenue may be running ahead of actual usage — watch renewal and engagement disclosure rather than seats sold.
insights.locator: I think you can see all of this in the experience of enterprise AI deployment

insights.claim: Handing every employee a chatbot is structurally the same move as giving everyone a PC and Lotus 123 in 1983 or a browser in 1997 — necessary, but not the mechanism by which invoice processing, supply chains or e-commerce were actually transformed.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Predicts a long lag between horizontal AI distribution and measurable enterprise productivity; sets expectations for 'where's the ROI' cycles.
insights.locator: it's mostly the same problem that you would have had

insights.claim: Roughly half of enterprise AI pilots work, which is the normal rate and precisely why they are called pilots.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Reframes widely-cited AI pilot failure statistics as unremarkable — a fade for headlines claiming enterprise AI is failing.
insights.locator: There’s now all sorts of data around how many of these pilots there are

insights.claim: Pilots do not scale arithmetically: a company with hundreds of workflows that has run five or ten pilots has barely started, which is why boards perceive a scaling problem the CIO's use-case playbook cannot solve.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Explains the gap between AI enthusiasm at board level and flat measured impact; the fix is process redesign spend, not more pilots.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, the CEO and the board scratch their heads

insights.claim: Workflows worth automating typically touch 50 or 500 people across five departments, three systems of record and four regulatory regimes, so an individual's AI-built tool cannot change how the company works — it requires a purchase, a decision and an 18-month sales process.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI revenue is gated by procurement cycles, not model releases — expect long, lumpy adoption curves.
insights.locator: Many of the problems, workflows and tasks that we might want to automate

insights.claim: The AI transition generates a wave of new pitches for professional services firms — Accenture for deploying an LLM voice-analytics tool in a call center, the Big Four for taking an AI startup to market, and Bain, BCG or McKinsey for the board-level existential question.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Systems integrators and strategy consultancies are a levered, under-discussed way to play enterprise AI adoption.
insights.locator: all of this means lots of new pitches for professional services

insights.claim: It is ironic that professional services firms profit from AI deployment while AI poses serious questions to their own headcount-based business models.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: A two-sided trade: near-term services revenue tailwind against a longer-term pyramid-model threat.
insights.locator: which is ironical given how many questions AI poses

insights.claim: The big AI labs are building their own deployment arms, such that a 'forward deployed engineer' is often just someone OpenAI hired out of a systems integrator.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Lab revenue is picking up services mix — relevant to how lab gross margins and valuation multiples should be read.
insights.quote: we used to joke that a ‘machine learning scientist’ is a statistician who lives in San Francisco, so maybe a ‘forward deployed engineer’ is anyone that OpenAI hired from a systems integrator
insights.locator: The vendors themselves have always been happy to help

insights.claim: Starting an 'AI-enabled' law firm may be the way to route around the difficulty of selling AI software into law and accountancy firms, but it may equally turn out like starting a 'PC-enabled law firm' in the 1980s.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Frames the AI-roll-up-of-services-firms trade as unresolved rather than obviously right.
insights.locator: go start an ‘AI-enabled’ law firm

themes.theme: Three questions and where the real value lands

insights.claim: Every company facing a transformative technology must answer three distinct questions: how to buy, build and deploy it; how far it changes their operations; and whether it creates new competitive pressure or an existential threat.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: A checklist for judging whether a company's AI messaging addresses economics and competitive threat or only deployment theatre.
insights.locator: Stepping back, it seems to me that with each new transformative technology

insights.claim: The operational answer to a new technology diverges radically by industry — what email or spreadsheets meant for an insurance company was entirely different from what they meant for a law firm.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Argues against uniform sector-level AI impact scores; dispersion within and across industries should be high.
insights.locator: Second, they have to ask how far this changes their operations

insights.claim: With every new technology we first do the work we already have faster, but the things that end up mattering in a platform shift are the ones that were not possible before and that no-one imagined.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Implies the biggest AI value creation will not show up in enterprise-productivity metrics or incumbent workflow automation, but in categories that do not yet exist.
insights.locator: Stepping back from all of this, though, there's also a much simpler way

insights.claim: Automating classes of work inside existing companies and workflows will be enormously more trouble and work than simply giving everybody a model.
insights.speaker: Benedict Evans
insights.so_what: Sets a slow base rate for AI-driven margin expansion at large incumbents; near-term AI P&L impact likely disappoints.
insights.locator: We will use AI to automate broad classes of stuff
